Maybe I ought to have started one! I was off to a start last fall when I reviewed 20 upper elementary books that were on the list for a 'Super Scholar Book Club.' Only one of the 20 had a traditional married Mother and Father as head of household, and they took in a foster street child! (Don't get touchy--not knocking the 2/3 of foster care that is decent—I'm just pointing out that all the "heroes" in the books had a big slice of dysfunction going on in the plots.) Fifteen of the books were less than three years old in the copyright and the oldest was written in 2003, which means they reflected "contemporary morality" which justifies a lot of behavior that the Bible does not. Some had occult themes and settings. I won't even go into the artwork except to say that very little of it could be described with the word pretty. All books pushed a liberal agenda at some level.

The thing that became obvious to me was that these books are not "market-driven" in same sense that my college economics of the 1980s taught— that is, the publishing houses are not making business decisions based on the preferences of the end-consumer, the parents of children that read the books. There are middle-men librarians and school administrators who are steering this. Homeschooling parents who have to pay for curriculum are not buying this crap.

If your desire is to find quality reading recommendations for children, (a) visit some parent-driven homeschooling forums (not publisher's "helpful" websites) these will have the best suggestions, and (b) add in some older classics.
